variants.name: Interface constraints with static abstract members (C# 11 / .NET 7)
variants.implementation_notes: A constrained type parameter is C#'s trait: where T : IComparable<T> requires the property, and C# 11's static abstract interface members extend the mechanism to statics and operators, so where T : IAdditionOperators<T,T,T> makes + available inside generic code - the shape .NET 7's generic-math interfaces (INumber<T>, INumberBase<T>) are built from, usually with the self-referencing where T : ISelf<T> pattern so the members can mention T. Reified generics mean typeof(T) also works at runtime, so a Type-keyed lookup remains possible, but the constraint form keeps selection at compile time and needs no reflection. For behaviour that really is per-type, an ordinary interface plus pattern matching (is/switch on type patterns) is what replaces the classic descriptor; the descriptor itself survives as the interface declaration.
pitfalls: Static abstract members are reachable only through a constrained type parameter: T.Min compiles, IRange<T>.Min does not, so code holding Type objects must fall back to reflection.

An interface with static abstract members cannot be used as a type argument unless every member has a most-specific implementation, and forgetting the self-referencing constraint (where T : IRange<T>) makes the trait unusable in generic methods.
The mechanism is nominal: a type must implement the interface, or you must write a wrapper struct, so a third-party type cannot be described from the outside the way a C++ specialization can.

variants.name: Instance interfaces and external comparers (C# 2 era)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C# 11 the only way to state a type property was an instance interface with a generic constraint (where T : IComparable<T>, where T : struct), which covers per-value behaviour but cannot express statics or operators at all - the language proposal for static abstracts says so explicitly. Ordering and similar properties were therefore supplied as an external object instead of a descriptor: IComparer<T> or a Comparison<T> delegate passed to List<T>.Sort, and a Dictionary<Type, Handler> (or a reflection lookup) as the fallback for describing a type that cannot be edited. Choose this form for libraries that must target .NET Framework or pre-.NET 7 runtimes.
pitfalls: Without static abstract members there is no way to abstract over operators, so arithmetic inside a constrained generic method has to be passed in as a delegate or an interface parameter.
An external comparer defines its own precedence: one that is inconsistent with Equals breaks hash-based collections and sorting contracts in ways the compiler cannot see.
A Type-keyed registry checks the runtime type only; a derived type silently misses the entry unless you walk the base classes and define a fallback.
